question: What specifically does G.S. 93A-13 bar absent a written, signed agreement for broker services?
choice_a: A broker's court action against the client to recover compensation under the agreement
choice_b: The broker's ability to hold an active real estate license
choice_c: The broker's ability to advertise the property at all
choice_d: The client's ability to sue the broker for negligence
explanation: G.S. 93A-13 provides that no action between a broker and the broker's client for recovery under an agreement for broker services is valid unless the contract is reduced to writing and signed by the party to be charged (or someone lawfully authorized to sign for that party).

question: Under G.S. 93A-13, whose signature is required for a broker-services contract to support a recovery action?
choice_a: The party to be charged (i.e., the party against whom recovery is sought), or another person lawfully authorized to sign for that party
choice_b: Both parties and a notary public
choice_c: Only the broker-in-charge of the firm, regardless of who represented the client
choice_d: The Real Estate Commission's executive director
explanation: G.S. 93A-13 requires the contract to be signed by the party to be charged or by some other person lawfully authorized by that party to sign -- it does not require both parties' signatures for the statute's purpose.

question: Besides brokerage-services agreements for sales and leases, what other type of agreement does Rule A.0104(a) also require to be in writing and signed?
choice_a: An agreement for services connected with the management of a property owners association
choice_b: Any agreement between two licensees to carpool to a showing
choice_c: An agreement to co-list a property with a broker from a different firm
choice_d: An informal referral of a customer between two brokers within the same firm
explanation: Rule A.0104(a) requires that every agreement for brokerage services in a real estate transaction, and every agreement for services connected with the management of a property owners association, be in writing and signed by the parties.

question: Under Rule A.0104(a), what must every written agreement for brokerage services specify regarding its length?
choice_a: A definite period of time
choice_b: An indefinite, open-ended term
choice_c: A term of exactly 12 months
choice_d: No term is required to be stated
explanation: Rule A.0104(a) requires every written agreement for brokerage services of any kind to be for a definite period of time.

question: As a general rule under Rule A.0104(a) (apart from the specific landlord-tenant-procurement exception), what must a written brokerage-services agreement provide regarding what happens at the end of its stated period?
choice_a: It shall provide for its termination without prior notice at the expiration of that period
choice_b: It shall automatically renew for an identical term unless the broker objects
choice_c: It shall require 90 days' advance notice from both parties before it can end
choice_d: It shall convert automatically into a dual agency agreement
explanation: As a general rule, Rule A.0104(a) requires that a written brokerage-services agreement provide for termination without prior notice at the expiration of its stated definite period; the automatic-renewal option for landlord/tenant-procurement agreements is a specific, narrow exception to this general rule.

question: If a written brokerage-services agreement includes a penalty for early termination, how must that provision be presented under Rule A.0104(a)?
choice_a: In a clear and conspicuous manner that distinguishes it from the other provisions of the agreement
choice_b: In the same typeface and location as every other clause, with no special emphasis
choice_c: Only in a separate document never shown to the client
choice_d: Verbally, at the time the agreement is signed, with no written record
explanation: Rule A.0104(a) requires that an early-termination-penalty provision in a written brokerage-services agreement be set forth in a clear and conspicuous manner that distinguishes it from the agreement's other provisions.

question: A buyer wants an EXCLUSIVE buyer agency agreement that restricts the buyer from working with other agents. Under Rule A.0104(a), may this agreement start out oral, the way a non-exclusive buyer agency agreement can?
choice_a: No -- any agreement that seeks to bind the buyer for a period of time or restrict the buyer's right to work with other agents must be in writing and signed from the outset
choice_b: Yes, as long as it is reduced to writing within a year
choice_c: Yes, all buyer agency agreements may begin orally regardless of exclusivity
choice_d: It depends solely on the purchase price of the property being sought
explanation: Rule A.0104(a) singles out agreements that bind a buyer/tenant for a period of time or restrict the buyer's/tenant's right to work with other agents (or without an agent) -- those must be in writing and signed by the parties from the start; only a non-exclusive, indefinite-term buyer/tenant agreement is permitted to begin orally.

question: Rule A.0104(a) requires that an agreement for brokerage services between a broker and a buyer or tenant be:
choice_a: Express, not merely implied from the parties' conduct
choice_b: Implied automatically once a broker shows the buyer three properties
choice_c: Presumed whenever a broker answers a buyer's question at an open house
choice_d: Unnecessary, since buyer agency cannot legally exist in North Carolina
explanation: Rule A.0104(a) requires that an agreement for brokerage services between a broker and a buyer or tenant be express -- an actual, stated agreement -- and, subject to the timing rules, in writing and signed by the parties.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven categories specified in the non-discrimination statement Rule A.0104(b) requires in every written agency agreement?
choice_a: Sexual orientation
choice_b: Handicap
choice_c: Familial status
choice_d: National origin
explanation: The Rule A.0104(b) statement covers race, color, religion, sex, national origin, handicap, and familial status. Sexual orientation is not one of the categories listed in this Commission rule.

question: Under Rule A.0104(c), what must be set forth directly on the 'Working with Real Estate Agents' publication itself when a broker gives it to a prospective buyer or seller?
choice_a: The broker's name and license number
choice_b: The broker's home mailing address
choice_c: The purchase price the broker expects the property to sell for
choice_d: The Real Estate Commission's office phone number
explanation: Rule A.0104(c) requires the broker to set forth their name and license number on the 'Working with Real Estate Agents' publication provided at first substantial contact.

question: A prospective buyer calls a real estate office only to ask what hours it is open, without discussing any specific property needs or financial information. Has 'first substantial contact' occurred under Rule A.0104(c)?
choice_a: No -- first substantial contact requires the discussion to begin focusing on the buyer's specific property needs, desires, or financial situation, which a general question about office hours does not do
choice_b: Yes -- any phone call to the office automatically triggers first substantial contact
choice_c: Yes -- because the buyer initiated contact
choice_d: It cannot be determined without knowing the buyer's name
explanation: A general inquiry, such as asking about office hours, does not itself trigger first substantial contact; that occurs once the discussion begins to focus on the prospective buyer's specific property needs, desires, or financial situation.

question: Under Rule A.0104(c), in addition to reviewing the 'Working with Real Estate Agents' publication with a prospective buyer or seller, what else must the broker do at first substantial contact?
choice_a: Determine whether the broker will act as agent of the buyer or of the seller in the transaction
choice_b: Immediately record the conversation and file it with the Commission
choice_c: Require the prospect to sign a binding listing agreement on the spot
choice_d: Refer the prospect to a different licensee at another firm
explanation: Rule A.0104(c) requires the broker, at first substantial contact, to provide and review the publication with the buyer or seller and to determine whether the broker will act as the agent of the buyer or of the seller in the transaction.

question: Under Rule A.0104(e), a broker working directly with a prospective buyer as a seller's agent or subagent must disclose in writing, at first substantial contact, that the broker represents the seller's interests -- and that disclosure must include what?
choice_a: The broker's license number
choice_b: The seller's Social Security number
choice_c: The commission split between the listing and selling firms
choice_d: A copy of the seller's mortgage payoff statement
explanation: Rule A.0104(e) requires a seller's agent or subagent working directly with a prospective buyer to disclose in writing at first substantial contact that they represent the seller's interests, and that written disclosure must include the broker's license number.

question: Under Rule A.0104(e), if a seller's agent's first substantial contact with a prospective buyer occurs by telephone or other electronic means where a written disclosure is not practical at that moment, what must the agent do?
choice_a: Transmit or mail the written disclosure to the buyer no later than three days from first substantial contact
choice_b: Nothing further is required once oral contact has occurred
choice_c: Wait until the closing table to provide any written disclosure
choice_d: The written disclosure requirement is waived entirely for electronic contact
explanation: Just as with the buyer-agent disclosure timing rule, Rule A.0104(e) requires that when first substantial contact occurs by telephone or electronic communication and written disclosure isn't practical at that time, the seller's agent must transmit or mail the written disclosure no later than three days from first substantial contact.

question: Under Rule A.0104(f), what must a buyer's agent's written confirmation of representation, delivered to the seller no later than the time an offer is delivered, include?
choice_a: The broker's license number
choice_b: The buyer's employer's name and address
choice_c: A copy of the buyer's credit report
choice_d: The buyer's Social Security number
explanation: Rule A.0104(f) requires the buyer's agent's written confirmation to the seller (or seller's agent), due no later than delivery of an offer to purchase, to include the broker's license number.
source_note: Disclosure of Agency Status by Buyers' Agents [Rule A.0104(f)]

question: When a buyer/tenant agency relationship has already been reduced to a written agreement (rather than remaining under the permitted oral, non-exclusive arrangement), by when must written authority for dual agency generally be obtained under Rule A.0104(d)?
choice_a: Upon the formation of the dual agency relationship (rather than being deferred until an offer is made, as is permitted only for a party still under an oral agreement)
choice_b: At any point up to one year after closing
choice_c: It is never required once a written buyer agency agreement already exists
choice_d: Only if the seller specifically demands it
explanation: Rule A.0104(d) requires written authority for dual agency to be obtained prior to undertaking to act as dual agent; deferring that written authority until the time an offer is made is a narrower allowance specifically tied to a party still represented under a permitted oral agency agreement.

question: Under Rule A.0104(j), before a firm may use designated agency in an in-house dual agency situation, what must it obtain?
choice_a: The prior express written approval of both clients
choice_b: A waiver from the Real Estate Commission's chairperson
choice_c: Nothing -- designated agency may be used automatically whenever a firm represents both parties
choice_d: Approval from the opposing firm's broker-in-charge
explanation: Rule A.0104(j) permits a firm to designate individual brokers to represent only the seller and only the buyer in an in-house dual agency situation, but only with the prior express written approval of both clients.

question: Under Rule A.0104(j), a firm may NOT designate a particular broker to represent one party in an in-house dual agency situation if that broker:
choice_a: Has actually received confidential information concerning the other party in connection with the transaction
choice_b: Has more than five years of licensure
choice_c: Works out of a branch office rather than the main office
choice_d: Has previously represented a buyer in an unrelated transaction
explanation: Rule A.0104(j) bars designating an individual broker to represent only one party if that broker has actually received confidential information concerning the other party in connection with the transaction.

question: Under Rule A.0104(j), the written designation of individual designated agents must be made no later than what point?
choice_a: No later than the point by which the parties' written dual agency authority itself must be obtained
choice_b: No later than 60 days after closing
choice_c: No later than the listing expiration date
choice_d: There is no deadline for making the designation in writing
explanation: Rule A.0104(j) ties the deadline for the written designated-agency authority to the same deadline that otherwise applies to obtaining written dual agency authority under Rule A.0104(d).

question: Under Rule A.0104(j), may a broker-in-charge (BIC) act as the designated broker for one party in a transaction where a provisional broker under that BIC's supervision is acting as the designated broker for the other, competing party?
choice_a: No -- a BIC may not act as a designated broker for a party in a transaction when a provisional broker under the BIC's supervision is acting as designated broker for a party with a competing interest
choice_b: Yes, without any restriction
choice_c: Yes, provided the BIC has more than ten years of experience
choice_d: Yes, as long as the transaction closes within 30 days
explanation: Rule A.0104(j) prohibits a broker-in-charge from acting as a designated broker for a party when a provisional broker under the BIC's supervision will act as designated broker for another party with a competing interest, given the BIC's supervisory authority over that provisional broker.

question: Under Rule A.0104(k) and (l), which three categories of information about their own client is a designated broker generally barred from disclosing to the other party (or that party's designated broker) without the client's permission?
choice_a: (1) That the client may accept a price, terms, or conditions other than those offered; (2) the client's motivation for engaging in the transaction; and (3) any information the client has identified as confidential
choice_b: (1) The client's name; (2) the client's phone number; and (3) the client's mailing address
choice_c: (1) The listing price; (2) the property address; and (3) the closing date
choice_d: (1) The broker's commission rate; (2) the broker's license number; and (3) the broker's firm name
explanation: Rules A.0104(k) and (l) bar a designated broker from disclosing, without permission: that the party may agree to a price, terms, or conditions other than those offered; the party's motivation for engaging in the transaction; and any information the party has identified as confidential.

question: Under Rule A.0104(k) and (l), when may a designated broker disclose their client's flexibility on price, motivation, or self-identified confidential information without the client's permission?
choice_a: When disclosure is otherwise required by statute or rule
choice_b: Whenever the designated broker believes it would speed up the transaction
choice_c: Never, under any circumstance
choice_d: Only after the transaction closes
explanation: The confidentiality protections in Rules A.0104(k) and (l) yield only where disclosure is otherwise required by statute or rule; absent such a requirement, the designated broker needs the client's permission.

question: Under Rule A.0104(m), by when must the identities of all the designated brokers in a transaction be disclosed to both parties?
choice_a: Before the first offer is made
choice_b: Within 10 days after closing
choice_c: Only if a party specifically requests the information
choice_d: Identities of designated brokers never need to be disclosed
explanation: Rule A.0104(m) requires that the identities of all designated brokers be disclosed to both parties before the first offer is made.

question: In an in-house designated dual agency, Designated Broker A represents the seller and Designated Broker B (from the same firm) represents the buyer. During negotiations, may Broker A actively advocate for the seller's interest in obtaining the highest achievable price, the way a single-party seller's agent normally would?
choice_a: Yes -- unlike a standard dual agent, who must remain neutral toward both parties, a designated broker may represent and advocate only for the interests of their own designated client
choice_b: No -- designated agents are held to the exact same neutrality standard as a standard dual agent
choice_c: No -- designated agents may not negotiate price at all
choice_d: Only if the firm's broker-in-charge personally approves each offer
explanation: The core purpose of designated agency is to restore each client's advocacy: unlike a standard dual agent, who must stay neutral and may not advocate for one client over the other, each designated broker represents and may advocate solely for their own designated client.

question: A broker holds a 10% ownership interest in a commercial property and wants to represent a prospective buyer of that same property. Under Rule A.0104(o), is this permitted?
choice_a: Yes -- because the ownership interest is under 25% and the property is commercial, the broker may represent the buyer if the buyer consents after full written disclosure of the ownership interest
choice_b: No -- any ownership interest, no matter how small, absolutely bars the broker from representing a buyer of that property
choice_c: Yes, automatically, with no disclosure or consent required
choice_d: No, because the exception under Rule A.0104(o) applies only to residential property
explanation: Rule A.0104(o) generally bars a broker with an ownership interest in a property from representing a buyer of it, but carves out an exception for commercial real estate where the broker's ownership interest is less than 25%, provided the buyer consents after full written disclosure of the interest.
source_note: Brokers As Parties to Transactions [Rule A.0104(o)]

question: Under Rule A.0104(o), at what ownership-interest threshold does a broker selling commercial real estate lose eligibility for the exception that would otherwise allow them to represent a buyer of that property?
choice_a: 25% or more
choice_b: 1% or more
choice_c: 50% or more
choice_d: There is no threshold -- any ownership interest qualifies for the exception
explanation: Rule A.0104(o)'s exception is limited to a broker selling commercial real estate with an ownership interest of less than 25 percent; at 25% or above, the exception does not apply.
source_note: Brokers As Parties to Transactions [Rule A.0104(o)]

question: Does the Rule A.0104(o) exception allowing a broker with a minority ownership interest to represent a buyer, after disclosure and consent, apply to residential property?
choice_a: No -- the exception applies only to commercial real estate, not residential property
choice_b: Yes -- it applies equally to residential and commercial property
choice_c: Yes, but only for residential property valued over $500,000
choice_d: The rule does not distinguish between property types
explanation: Rule A.0104(o)'s narrow exception (allowing representation of a buyer despite a broker's ownership interest, with disclosure and consent) is limited to brokers selling commercial real estate; it does not extend to residential property.
source_note: Brokers As Parties to Transactions [Rule A.0104(o)]

question: A listing broker wants to purchase the property they have listed but has not yet made any written disclosure to the seller about the potential conflict of interest. Under Rule A.0104(p), may the broker proceed directly to a purchase contract?
choice_a: No -- the broker must first make the required written disclosure (and advise the seller to consider independent counsel) before any purchase contract may be entered into
choice_b: Yes, as long as the broker pays fair market value
choice_c: Yes, because listing brokers are automatically exempt from this rule
choice_d: Yes, provided the purchase closes within 24 hours
explanation: Rule A.0104(p) prohibits a listing broker or firm from purchasing a listed property unless they first disclose in writing that a potential conflict of interest exists and that the seller may want independent counsel -- entering a purchase contract before this disclosure is not permitted.
source_note: Brokers As Parties to Transactions [Rule A.0104(p)]

question: After a listing broker makes the required written conflict-of-interest disclosure under Rule A.0104(p), what must happen to the listing itself before the broker/firm may enter into a purchase contract for the property?
choice_a: The listing must be terminated, or transferred to another broker
choice_b: Nothing further -- the disclosure alone is sufficient
choice_c: The listing price must be reduced by at least 10%
choice_d: The listing must be extended for an additional year
explanation: Rule A.0104(p) requires that, after the written disclosure, the listing broker/firm terminate the listing agreement or transfer it to another broker before entering into a contract to purchase the listed property.
source_note: Brokers As Parties to Transactions [Rule A.0104(p)]

question: Under Rule A.0108, for how long must a broker generally retain records such as agency agreements and disclosure documents connected with a transaction?
choice_a: Three years after all funds held by the broker in connection with the transaction have been disbursed, or the conclusion of the transaction, whichever occurs later
choice_b: One year from the date the listing agreement was signed, with no exceptions
choice_c: There is no minimum retention period
choice_d: Permanently, for the life of the brokerage firm
explanation: Rule A.0108 requires brokers to retain transaction records, including agency contracts and disclosure documents, for three years after all held funds have been disbursed or the transaction concluded, whichever is later.

question: Under Rule A.0108, if an agency agreement is terminated before the transaction concludes, from what point does the record-retention period for that agreement run?
choice_a: Three years from the termination of the agency agreement, or the disbursement of all held funds, whichever occurs later
choice_b: The retention requirement disappears entirely once the agreement is terminated
choice_c: Three years from the original date the listing was first advertised
choice_d: One year from termination, with no reference to fund disbursement
explanation: Rule A.0108 specifies that if the agency agreement is terminated before the transaction's conclusion, records must be kept for three years after the agreement's termination or the disbursement of all held funds, whichever occurs later.

question: Comparing the timing rules that generally apply to an ordinary (non-auction) sales transaction, which statement correctly relates the WWREA agency disclosure deadline under Rule A.0104(c) to the written buyer agency agreement deadline under Rule A.0104(a)?
choice_a: The WWREA disclosure is generally required at first substantial contact, which is typically earlier in the relationship than the written buyer agency agreement, which is not required until no later than the time an offer is made
choice_b: The written buyer agency agreement is always required before any WWREA disclosure can lawfully be given
choice_c: Both deadlines fall on the exact same event -- the closing of the transaction
choice_d: Neither deadline has any defined trigger point under the rules
explanation: Under Rule A.0104(c), agency disclosure (the WWREA brochure) is triggered at first substantial contact, an earlier point in the relationship, while under Rule A.0104(a) the written buyer/tenant agency agreement need not be signed until no later than the time either party makes an offer.
source_note: Agency Agreements & Agency Disclosure Requirement [Rule A.0104(a), (c)]

question: Which of the following is NOT a requirement Rule A.0104(a) imposes on every written agreement for brokerage services of any kind?
choice_a: Approval of the agreement's terms in advance by the Real Estate Commission
choice_b: The agreement must be for a definite period of time
choice_c: The agreement must include the broker's license number
choice_d: The agreement must provide for termination without prior notice at the expiration of that period
explanation: Rule A.0104(a) requires a definite term, inclusion of the broker's license number, and a provision for termination without prior notice at expiration -- it does not require the Commission to pre-approve the agreement's terms.
